title: He Mastered Every Tactical Rule of Chess, Yet Could Not Remember Playing One Single Game
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Endel Tulving (1972/2002): 'Mental Time Travel' — Patient K.C. Knowing Every Rule of Chess Without Remembering Playing a Single Game, grounded in Endel Tulving (2002) (Annual Review of Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1972, University of Toronto psychologist Endel Tulving proposed a bold split inside conscious declarative memory that many doubted at first: Semantic Memory (timeless encyclopedia facts: 'Paris is the capital of France; bishops move diagonally') versus Episodic Memory ('Mental Time Travel' — stepping back inside a specific moment you personally lived: 'The rainy Tuesday in Paris when we dropped our baguette').

At the circuit level, this episode examines how temporal lobe, hippocampus, default mode network coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that nature delivered astonishing living proof in Toronto: in 1981, 30-year-old Kent Cochrane ('Patient K.C.') suffered severe head trauma in a motorcycle crash that destroyed his bilateral hippocampi alongside parahippocampal and medial frontoparietal lesions.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Endel Tulving (2002). Episodic Memory: From Mind to Brain. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.psych.53.100901.135114
- Francis Eustache (2023). Memory according to Endel Tulving. Revue de neuropsychologie. https://doi.org/10.1684/nrp.2023.0773
- Daniel L. Schacter, Donna Rose Addis, Randy L. Buckner (2007). Remembering the past to imagine the future: the prospective brain. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn2213

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
